---
title: "Who Gets a Summons? Toronto Marijuana Arrests, 1997 to 2002"
output:
  flexdashboard::flex_dashboard:
    theme: flatly
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5)
library(flexdashboard)
source("_setup.R")
```

The Story {.storyboard}
=======================================================================

### **1. Black arrestees were less likely than White arrestees to be released with a summons** (`r pct(rate(A$colour == "Black"))` versus `r pct(rate(A$colour == "White"))`).

```{r s1, fig.width = 6.5}
plot_release_by_colour()
```

***

**The data.** `r scales::comma(nrow(A))` arrests for simple possession of marijuana in Toronto, 1997 to 2002 (`carData::Arrests`). After arrest, police either released the person with a summons to appear in court or held them for a bail hearing. Being held is the harsher outcome.

**The finding.** `r pct(rate(A$colour == "White"), 1)` of White arrestees were released compared with `r pct(rate(A$colour == "Black"), 1)` of Black arrestees. Put another way, Black arrestees were held `r sprintf("%.1f", (1 - rate(A$colour == "Black")) / (1 - rate(A$colour == "White")))` times as often. The crude odds ratio for release (White versus Black) is `r fmt_or(or_crude)`.

**Transition.** A difference in release rates could reflect how police treat Black and White arrestees. It could also reflect other ways in which the two groups of arrestees differ. The next frame looks at those differences.

### **2. Black arrestees differed from White arrestees.** They were more often unemployed and non citizens, and more often appeared in police databases.

```{r s2}
plot_profile_by_colour()
```

***

**The finding.** Compared with White arrestees, Black arrestees were

* more often unemployed (`r pct(mean(A$employed[A$colour == "Black"] == "No"))` versus `r pct(mean(A$employed[A$colour == "White"] == "No"))`)
* more often non citizens (`r pct(mean(A$citizen[A$colour == "Black"] == "No"))` versus `r pct(mean(A$citizen[A$colour == "White"] == "No"))`)
* more often in 3 or more police databases (`r pct(mean(A$checks[A$colour == "Black"] >= 3))` versus `r pct(mean(A$checks[A$colour == "White"] >= 3))`).

The two groups had a similar sex mix. White arrestees were somewhat younger (`r pct(mean(A$age[A$colour == "White"] < 21))` under 21 versus `r pct(mean(A$age[A$colour == "Black"] < 21))`), but age is only weakly related to release.

**Transition.** These differences only matter for the colour gap if employment, citizenship and police checks also affect who gets released.

### **3. Employment, citizenship and especially police checks strongly predicted release.**

```{r s3}
plot_release_drivers()
```

***

**The finding.**

* `r pct(rate(A$employed == "Yes"))` of employed versus `r pct(rate(A$employed == "No"))` of unemployed arrestees were released.
* `r pct(rate(A$citizen == "Yes"))` of citizens versus `r pct(rate(A$citizen == "No"))` of non citizens were released.
* Release fell steadily with each additional police check, from `r pct(rate(A$checks == 0))` with none to about `r pct(rate(A$checks >= 4))` with four or more.

Sex, age and year were only weakly related to release (see the Appendix).

**Transition.** Because Black arrestees were more often in the groups that police released less often, part of the colour gap in frame 1 could be due to these differences. To check, we compare Black and White arrestees who share the same employment and citizenship status.

### **4. The colour gap remained within every employment and citizenship group.**

```{r s4}
plot_colour_within_groups()
```

***

**The finding.** In each of the four employment and citizenship groups, White arrestees were released more often than Black arrestees, by roughly 7 to 12 percentage points. The gap is about the same size in every group. A logistic model with all interactions among colour, employment and citizenship fits no better than one with main effects alone (`r fmt_p(lrt_cec[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2])`).

Release ranged from `r pct(min(rel_by(A, colour, employed, citizen)$p))` for Black, unemployed non citizens to `r pct(max(rel_by(A, colour, employed, citizen)$p))` for White, employed citizens.

**Transition.** This comparison does not account for police checks, the strongest predictor of release. A regression model can account for checks and every other variable at the same time.

### **5. After accounting for all other variables, White arrestees still had about `r sprintf("%.1f", or_adj[1])` times the odds of release.**

```{r s5}
plot_forest()
```

***

**The finding.** The odds ratio for release (White versus Black) falls from `r fmt_or(or_crude)` to `r fmt_or(or_adj)` after adjusting for year, age, sex, employment, citizenship and checks. About half of the crude gap (on the log odds scale) is explained by these variables, mainly checks and employment. The rest remains.

Each additional police check multiplies the odds of release by about `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(coef(fit_adj)["checks"]))`. Employment roughly doubles the odds, and citizenship raises them by about 80%.

**Transition.** A single odds ratio is an average over all arrestees. The last step asks whether the colour gap is the same for everyone.

### **6. The colour gap was concentrated among younger arrestees and in the earlier years.**

```{r s6}
plot_age_period()
```

***

**The finding.** Adding colour by age and colour by year interactions to the adjusted model clearly improves fit (χ² = `r sprintf("%.1f", lrt_int$Deviance[2])` on `r lrt_int$Df[2]` df, `r fmt_p(lrt_int[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2])`).

* In 1997 to 1999, young Black arrestees were released about 20 percentage points less often than young White arrestees.
* In 2000 to 2002 the gap narrowed for most ages.
* Among arrestees over 40, Black arrestees were released at least as often as White arrestees in both periods.

**Transition.** The final frame brings the steps together.

### **7. Conclusion.** A colour gap in release that background differences explain only in part, and that varies by age and over time.

```{r s7}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Step, ~Finding, ~`Key number`,
  "1", "Black arrestees were released less often", paste(pct(rate(A$colour == "Black")), "vs", pct(rate(A$colour == "White"))),
  "2", "Black arrestees were more often unemployed, non citizens and in police databases", paste("3+ checks:", pct(mean(A$checks[A$colour == "Black"] >= 3)), "vs", pct(mean(A$checks[A$colour == "White"] >= 3))),
  "3", "Those characteristics strongly predict release", paste("0 checks", pct(rate(A$checks == 0)), "vs 4+ checks", pct(rate(A$checks >= 4))),
  "4", "The gap remained within employment and citizenship groups", "7 to 12 points in every group",
  "5", "The gap was reduced but remained after full adjustment", paste("OR", sprintf("%.2f", or_crude[1]), "to", sprintf("%.2f", or_adj[1])),
  "6", "The gap was largest for young arrestees and in 1997 to 1999", paste("Interaction", fmt_p(lrt_int[["Pr(>Chi)"]][2]))
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

***

**Main message.** Among people arrested for marijuana possession in Toronto, Black arrestees were less likely to be released with a summons. About half of this gap is explained by differences in employment, citizenship and police record. The remaining gap was concentrated among young people and narrowed after 1999.

**Cautions for interpretation**

* **Selection.** The data include only people who were arrested, and Black residents are over represented among arrestees. These comparisons are conditional on arrest.
* **Checks may be a mediator.** If Black residents are more heavily policed, they will build up more database entries for the same behaviour. Adjusting for checks may then understate the total effect of colour.
* **Unmeasured factors**, such as quantity possessed, demeanour and outstanding warrants, are not recorded. The adjusted gap shows an association and does not by itself establish discrimination.
* **Odds ratios are not risk ratios** here, because the outcome is common (`r pct(1 - overall)` were held).

Storyboard Plan
=======================================================================

Column {data-width=500}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### Steps 1 and 2. Collect plots and group related findings

All tables and plots from the exploratory analysis are collected in `arrests_exploration.Rmd` (figures E1 to E12 and table T1). They form five groups.

| Group | Figures | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Who is arrested** | E1 | Arrestees are mostly young, male, White, employed and citizens. Black people are over represented relative to Toronto's population. Age is right skewed, checks are lumpy, and 1997 and 2002 are partial years. |
| **B. One at a time predictors of release** | E2, E3, E4, E5 | Release is lower for Black, unemployed and non citizen arrestees and falls with police checks. Sex, age and year matter little. |
| **C. How Black and White arrestees differ** | E8, E9, E10 | Black arrestees are more often unemployed and non citizens and have more police checks. |
| **D. The colour gap after accounting for other variables** | E6, E7, T1, E11 | The gap remains within subgroups and after full adjustment, at about half its crude size. |
| **E. Who the gap affects** | E12 | The gap is largest for young arrestees and in 1997 to 1999. |

E2 (release by colour) is duplicated from group B into the opening of the story because it states the problem.

### Step 3. The argument

**Starting point.** Black arrestees were less likely to be released (E2).

**End point.** A substantial gap remains after accounting for other differences, and it is concentrated among young arrestees in the earlier years (E11, E12).

**Intermediate steps needed.** To show that the adjusted gap is meaningful, the reader first needs to see that (i) Black and White arrestees differ on other characteristics, (ii) those characteristics predict release, and (iii) the gap still appears when like is compared with like. This is the logic of confounding. Groups C and B supply (i) and (ii), and group D supplies (iii).

Column {data-width=500}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### Step 4. Choose the plots needed

| Decision | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Keep** E2, E10, E7, E11, E12 | Each is a necessary step in the argument. |
| **Add** a new plot of release by employment, citizenship and checks (frame 3) | This was a hole in the argument. E3 and E4 spread these three predictors across two figures and mix them with weak predictors. |
| **Use** E10, the profile of Black and White arrestees, for frame 2 | E8 shows the same associations, but a four way mosaic is hard to read for a general audience. |
| **Drop** E3 from the story | Replaced by the new frame 3. |
| **Move to appendix** E1, E4, E5, E6, E8, E9 | Supplementary. E5 (spine plots) repeats E3. E6 (doubledecker) repeats E7, so only the clearer E7 stays in the story. E9 is summarised by one row of E10. |
| **Summarise in text only** sex, age and year main effects, T1 | These are weak predictors or repeat a plot, and they do not change the argument. |

### Step 5. Sequence

The story order is **not** the order of the analysis. The analysis went from distributions (Q1) to one at a time associations (Q2) to joint effects (Q3) and finally other features (Q4). The story instead **opens with the colour gap**, because that is the question a reader cares about. Each frame then answers the question raised by the previous one:

1. Is there a gap? Yes (E2).
2. Could it be explained by other differences? The groups do differ (E10).
3. Do those differences matter for release? Yes (new frame 3).
4. Does the gap survive comparing like with like? Yes (E7).
5. How big is it after accounting for everything? About half the crude size (E11).
6. Is it the same for everyone? No (E12).
7. Conclusion and cautions.

### Step 6. Captions and transitions

Every frame title is a full sentence caption stating the message of the plot. Each commentary panel ends with a **Transition** that poses the question answered by the next frame.

Appendix {.storyboard}
=======================================================================

### **A1. Who was arrested.** Mostly young, male, White, employed and citizens. 1997 and 2002 are partial years.

```{r a1, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_distributions()
```

***

Exploration figure E1 (Question 1). This gives context for the story but is not part of the main argument.

* Only `r pct(mean(A$sex == "Female"), 1)` of arrestees are female.
* `r pct(mean(A$colour == "Black"), 1)` are Black, compared with roughly 8% of Toronto's population in 2001.
* Age is right skewed (median `r median(A$age)`, range `r min(A$age)` to `r max(A$age)`).
* `r pct(mean(A$checks == 0))` have no police checks, with a second peak at 3.
* 1997 and 2002 have far fewer arrests than the middle years.

### **A2. Release by checks, age and year.** Checks has a strong gradient. Age and year have weak ones.

```{r a2, fig.height = 6}
grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(2, 2)))
print(plot_rate_by(rel_by(A, x = checks), "Number of checks", "Checks"),
      vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(plot_rate_by(rel_by(A, x = agegrp), "Age group", "Age"),
      vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))
print(plot_rate_by(rel_by(A, x = year), "Year", "Year"),
      vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = 1:2))
```

***

Exploration figure E4 (Question 2). The checks panel is summarised in story frame 3. Age and year are weak predictors on their own, but they modify the colour gap (story frame 6).

### **A3. Spine plots of release against each variable.**

```{r a3, fig.height = 6}
plot_spines()
```

***

Exploration figure E5 (Question 2). Bar width shows group size and the red segment shows the proportion held. It carries the same message as story frames 1 and 3, so it is kept here as supplementary detail.

### **A4. Doubledecker plot of release by citizenship, employment and colour.**

```{r a4, fig.height = 6}
plot_doubledecker()
```

***

Exploration figure E6 (Question 3). It shows the same result as story frame 4, and also how few arrestees fall in the non citizen groups. The dumbbell plot in frame 4 was preferred because the colour gap is easier to read there.

### **A5. Mosaic plot of colour, employment, citizenship and release.**

```{r a5, fig.height = 6}
plot_mosaic()
```

***

Exploration figure E8 (Question 3). Cells are shaded by Pearson residuals from the model of mutual independence. Blue cells hold more arrests than independence predicts, red cells fewer. It shows that the predictors are associated with each other, which story frame 2 conveys more simply.

### **A6. Distribution of police checks by colour.**

```{r a6}
plot_checks_by_colour()
```

***

Exploration figure E9 (Question 4). Mean checks are `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(A$checks[A$colour == "Black"]))` for Black and `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(A$checks[A$colour == "White"]))` for White arrestees. Story frame 2 summarises this as the share with 3 or more checks.
